zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid: the supplied Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). This review supplies its own scan-based transcription decisions and English notes; the index is not a diplomatic authority.

lines.note: This completes the figurative sense of Minacami begun on f0319: the beginning or origin of something. The earlier catchword Princi- anticipates this row; it is not repeated here as additional dictionary text.
Minacotogotocu means all or everything, matching Tudo. The scan retains the initial M omitted by OCR, and the entry begins at the headword margin rather than at continuation indentation.

The Japanese explanation Mite i nagara expresses doing something while looking; the Portuguese starts “as I am seeing.” Preserve the printed spaces in that explanation and the sharp-s-shaped ß in Aßi.

runs.text: vendo. ¶ Item, Todas as couſas jun

lines.note: Vendo finishes the first gloss. The pilcrow introduces a second, collective sense, “all things together”; jun continues into tas on the next row without a visible printed hyphen.
Tas completes juntas from the preceding row. The following P. labels this collective usage as poetic; its upright setting is separated from the italic Portuguese.

The verb describes a river running with force. Correr has a worn rounded o rather than the OCR e; the printed principal-part sequence u, itta is retained rather than regularized to a modern conjugation.
The example describes an exceptionally violent rushing flood. Cô- continues as zui on the next row; its upward-pointing long-vowel mark and the printed hyphen are retained.

Zui completes the Japanese word for flood, followed by the upright citation Taif. and an italic reference to book 25. The scan shows a stop after both the citation and the book number; dago- continues into as in the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: as que correm com grande impeto, & furia.

lines.note: This completes the translation as a flood of waters running with great force and fury. As belongs to the preceding dago-, not to a separate Japanese example.
This compound adds downward movement: a river descends violently. Preserve Decer and the joined printing orio rather than modernizing the spelling or silently inserting a word space.
Furia completes the gloss of Minaguiri cudari, “with fury.” This short continuation is a genuine physical row, not furniture or an omitted part of the following entry.
The compound describes water issuing or surging out. Sairo represents the printed joining of Sair and o; the historical principal parts zzuru, eta are preserved.
This completes the description of the river coming out with great force and flooding. The row belongs to Minaguiri ide rather than to the next compound.

The meaning is to flow violently, here said of a river. The damaged initial M is one ordinary-size letter, not the OCR B plus italic l; the first n of nagare has lost much of its right side. Nagare is adopted from the surviving traces together with the compound's sense and the supplied lexical index, with the damage left explicit here.
“With fury” completes the gloss of Minaguiri nagare. No additional headword or separate example is present on this short continuation row.
Minagurenai denotes something wholly red. Vt introduces the example of an entirely red fan on the following row.
The example is an all-red fan; the caron in vǒgui is visible and is not converted to a circumflex. The Portuguese ver- is completed by the displaced melho. printed at the far right of the next row.

Minami is the southern direction. The far-right parenthesis and melho. do not qualify “south”: they finish vermelho from the previous fan example. They are restored as right-aligned segments on this physical row, not relocated into its predecessor or treated as another row.
The repeated form means all people or all things. The gloss distinguishes the plural “all” from the collective “everything” without introducing an example.
Minamoto is the beginning or source of a river, also expressed here as a spring. The next row extends that concrete sense to origins more generally.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Origem, ou principio dalguã couſa.

lines.note: The pilcrow introduces the extended meaning, the origin or beginning of anything. The nasal mark is printed over the final a in dalguã here; it is not moved to match dalgũa elsewhere on the page.
Minamotte means everything or everyone. Both narrow t types are present; the OCR reading Minamotre confuses the second t with r. The doubled spelling also agrees with the supplied headword index.
Minarai means to learn by observing. The two principal-part vowels bear downward-pointing marks; Cǒ- begins the example's word for today and continues as nichi in the next row.

runs.text: nichi Muſaxiga ſuru icuſa coſo tefonyo,

lines.note: Together with Cǒ-, the example says that the battle fought by Musashi today is a model to follow. Preserve Muſaxi and the printed sequence tefonyo rather than substituting modern Japanese romanization.

The example concludes with an instruction to observe and learn well, followed by the upright citation Taca. The Portuguese translation begins “the battle which today”; preserve the fused Abatalha and historical oje.

runs.text: tem Benquei he exemplo, & modelo, vendo

lines.note: The translation calls Benquei's battle an example and model. The last letter of Benquei is dotted i, not the OCR l; the Japanese name occurs within italic Portuguese prose and is left in that printed typeface.
This finishes the translation's command to learn well by watching. The imperative belongs to the quotation and does not supply another principal part of Minarai.
Minare means becoming accustomed to a sight, or seeing something repeatedly. Its continuative gloss proceeds onto the next row.
The continuation specifies repeated seeing by habit. The final vowel of coſtume is e in the scan, correcting the OCR coſtuma without modernizing the long-s spelling.

runs.text: P. Vara de que vſão os homẽs

lines.note: This poetic entry names a pole used by seamen. P. is retained with the slanted Portuguese setting here; the nasal abbreviation in homẽs is visible.
The continuation specifies men of the sea using the pole aboard a vessel. It completes Minarezauo, not the fruit-bearing verb that follows.
Minari means to bear fruit. The register label S. is upright; the example begins Futa-, continued as tabi, meaning twice.

runs.text: tabi minaru qiua ſono ne canarazu itamu.

lines.note: The example says that a tree which bears fruit twice necessarily damages its roots. Qiua is the printed tree-plus-topic sequence; it is not split into modern transliteration units.

runs.text: Aruore que duas vazes no anno da

lines.note: The upright Feiq. introduces the cited example's Portuguese rendering, a tree bearing fruit twice in a year. Vazes is the scan's spelling, with a visible a, and is not silently changed to vezes.

runs.text: fruito, ſem falta ſe dana, ou a podrece.

lines.note: The translation says that such a tree inevitably becomes damaged or rots. Preserve the printed separation a podrece and the source's fruito spelling.

runs.text: Minari yoi, l, varui mono. l,

lines.note: This noun concerns outward appearance, illustrated by something or someone looking good or bad. The printed l, alternatives continue into coto on the next row; this is distinct from the preceding verb “bear fruit.”

runs.text: Peſſoa, ou couſa que parece bem à vis

lines.note: Coto finishes the Japanese alternatives; the Portuguese explains a person or thing that looks good to the eye. The line ends with a visible s in vis, not the OCR hyphen after vi; no printed hyphen is inserted before the next row's ta.
Ta completes vista from vis on the previous row. “Or badly” supplies the contrasting unfavorable appearance in the Minari example.
Minato is a port. The pilcrow introduces an example meaning to arrive at a port, whose Portuguese translation starts on the following row.
The first phrase translates arriving at port; the next Japanese example means bringing a vessel into port. Both the pilcrow and the transition from italic Portuguese to upright Japanese are retained.
This translates the preceding example as putting the vessel into port. It is a complete continuation row rather than a new entry.

runs.text: Foz do rio que entra no mar, ou

lines.note: Minatogaua is glossed in terms of the mouth of a river entering the sea. The alternative introduced by ou continues on the next row.

runs.text: que eſta na boca dalgum rio.

lines.note: The second description refers to something at a river's mouth. Preserve the source's relative-clause wording rather than smoothing its relation to the preceding definition.

runs.text: Cordas com que alão, ou aleuantão

lines.note: Minaua names ropes used to haul or raise a mast. The two nasal endings in alão and aleuantão are retained with the historical v/u spelling.
The object being hauled or raised is the mast. The printed maſto is kept, rather than modernized to mastro.

runs.text: Ver hũa couſa bem, ou mal

lines.note: Minaxi concerns viewing or judging a thing favorably or unfavorably. The gloss continues into interpretation on the next row and then into a cross-column example.

runs.text: deitandoa a boa, ou mà parte. ¶

lines.note: The continuation explains putting a good or bad construction on something. Iennin- begins the example's “good people”; the two abraded n types are read separately rather than as the OCR m+n, while the initial printed I is retained. The example continues at the top of column 2.

runs.text: ua fitono cǒxeqiuo yô minaxi, acuninua

lines.note: This continues Iennin- from the foot of column 1: good people interpret others' actions favorably, in contrast to bad people. The different marks on cǒ and yô are preserved rather than made uniform.

runs.text: Os juſtos vem as obras dos

lines.note: The Japanese contrast concludes that bad people construe them unfavorably. The Portuguese begins its matching account of the just seeing other people's actions; the printed plural vem is not modernized.

runs.text: outros deitandoas à boa parte, & os maos as

lines.note: The just interpret the actions of others favorably, while the bad do otherwise. The grave accent belongs to à; maos is retained without supplying a nasal sign absent from this printing.
The translation ends with the bad assigning an unfavorable interpretation. Preserve the joined amà and its grave accent rather than regularizing the phrase's spacing.
Minaxigo denotes orphans. The Portuguese plural has its nasal mark on o in Orfaõs, and that carrier is not modernized.

The poetic month name is explained by Rocuguachi, the sixth month. The introductory P. i, belongs to the slanted apparatus; the complete Japanese synonym is upright, including the flourished capital R that OCR partly italicized.
The continuation specifies the sixth lunar month of Japan, not automatically the Gregorian month of June. The tilde in lũa is kept as printed.

The synonym Tamino iye explains Minca as common people's houses; the Portuguese specifies farmers' houses. The synonym is not an embedded Portuguese term and is therefore not marked for the special term-toggle list.
Mincan means the populace or common people. Enlargement shows the upper bridge of n after Mi, correcting OCR u; the bilingual sense and the supplied headword index agree with that reading.
Mine first means a mountain summit. The pilcrow then introduces the related ridge or back of a sword, with mi- continued as ne on the next row.

Ne completes the sword example. The Portuguese calls this the sharp or ridged back of the Catana; retain its wording rather than replacing it with a modern technical definition. Catana is a Japanese-derived term within the italic gloss.
The entry describes passage along mountain summits. Preserve the printed douori, sharp-s form in Paßagem, and abbreviated nasal spelling mõtes.

runs.text: Corda de ſerras, ou cumes de

lines.note: Minetçuzzuqi is a connected range or chain of mountain ridges. The cedilla and doubled z belong to the printed Japanese spelling, not to a typographical correction.
This finishes the description of summits continuing in a chain. An actual n is visible in montes, correcting the OCR motes without substituting the nasal-abbreviated spelling found in another entry.

runs.text: O ir pellos montes, ou ſerras de

lines.note: Minezzutai means going along mountains or ridges. The next row supplies the movement from one to another.
The phrase completes the movement along ridges “from one to another.” The nasal abbreviation in hũa is retained rather than expanded into uma.

runs.text: O fugir ſò com a viſta do inimigo.

lines.note: Minigue describes fleeing at the mere sight of an enemy. The grave accent on ſò and the long-s spelling in viſta are preserved.
The construction with ſuru gives the act of fleeing on sight. Its Portuguese translation continues with “enemy” on the next physical row.
Inimigo completes the preceding example's translation. This single-word row is an ordinary continuation, not a catchword.
Minmet is explained through Meſſuru and the Portuguese “destruction.” The clipped final t is part of the historical headword; S. identifies written usage and is kept upright after the italic gloss.
Mino is a rain cape, followed by an example meaning to put one on. The Portuguese historical phrase capa dagoa is retained without inserting an apostrophe or changing its vowels.

runs.text: ou veſtir capa dagoa de Iapão.

lines.note: The continuation explains putting on or wearing a Japanese rain cape. This completes the clothing sense, which is distinct from the place-name Mino in the next two entries.
Minogami is paper from the region called Mino. The geographical name occurs inside the italic Portuguese definition and is marked for optional whole-word typeface review.

The Japanese compound concerns kaki fruit from Mino, while the Portuguese source calls the fruit figos. Preserve that historical categorization and the absence of a clear final stop; do not silently substitute a modern fruit name or punctuation.
Minogaxi is allowing something to escape despite seeing it, hence overlooking it. The next example applies that sense to faults rather than to literal flight.

The example says that faults were overlooked four or five times. The scan supports the object sequence Ayamariuo and the verb minogaita, correcting the OCR Ayamarito and manogaita; Diſ- begins the translation continued below.

The translation says that faults were passed over four or five times. The first numeral is visibly 4 followed by a stop, not OCR a followed by a comma. Fitouo begins a second example with a person as object; the historical Diſ- plus ſimoloulhe is not respelled.

runs.text: Deixar a alguem que ſe acolha,

lines.note: The second example means allowing a person to escape or take refuge. The initial vowel of alguem is an a; the preceding separate a is retained, correcting only the OCR olguem.
“And get free” finishes the second translation. It remains attached to letting someone escape, not to the wiping cloth in the next entry.

runs.text: Catabira ou toalha cõ que ſe a lim-

lines.note: Minogoi is a cloth for wiping the body, glossed using Catabira or a towel. Catabira is embedded in italic Portuguese; the visible spacing a lim- and the nasal abbreviation cõ are preserved.

runs.text: pa o corpo de pois de lauado.

lines.note: This finishes the description of wiping the body after washing. Pa completes lim- across the row break; de pois remains separated as printed.

runs.text: Minoqedachi, tçu, atta. l, minoqega tatçu.

lines.note: The entry gives both an inflected verb and an alternative phrase for the body's hair standing up. The source's alternative marker l, and the initial lowercase m of the second form are preserved.

runs.text: Arrepiaremſe os cabelos com frio, ou com me-

lines.note: The first gloss covers hair standing on end from cold or fear. Me- continues as do on the next row, where a further Japanese construction begins.
Do completes medo. The pilcrow introduces another expression for hair standing on end; preserve the printed separation Mino qega rather than joining it to match the preceding form.

runs.text: rem ſe os cabelos sò com medo.

lines.note: The second construction is restricted here to fear. Preserve the separated rem ſe and the grave accent on sò instead of normalizing the expression.
Minori means bearing fruit. No clear comma is printed between the headword and u, so the baseline's space is retained. Minora- begins the negative modifier of a tree in the following example.

runs.text: nu q uoba qitte fini cubeyo.

lines.note: The sense is “cut down the tree that bears no fruit and put it in the fire.” After Minora-nu the tree word would normally be qi, but the scan presents q followed by a conspicuous blank and uoba, with no secure i trace. The visible q uoba is retained without supplying the expected letter; the Portuguese A aruo- begins the confirming translation.

runs.text: re que não dà fruito, cortãdoa metea no fogo.

lines.note: This completes the translation: the tree that bears no fruit is to be cut and put in the fire. Preserve the grave in dà, nasal abbreviation cortãdoa, and joined metea.
Mintocu, explained as Taminotocu, denotes benefit or advantage to the people. The definition narrows this to farmers on the next row.
The continuation specifies benefits to farmers and marks written usage with upright S. The obscured but rounded o in lauradores corrects OCR lauradares; no modern u/v normalization is made.
Minvocu is explained as houses of the people. Tamino iye is a Japanese synonym, not an embedded term in the Portuguese sentence.
The alternative identifies the people here as farmers. This short line completes the house entry and does not qualify the following verb.

runs.text: Ver atè o interior, ou pene-

lines.note: Minuqi means seeing into the interior or penetrating with one's sight. The grave in atè and the physical break pene- are preserved.

The gloss concludes “penetrate with the sight”; the example begins a claim about seeing through a person's inner parts. Preserve the caron in gozǒuo and the transition from Portuguese italics to Japanese roman.

The two Japanese forms express seeing through the person's inward qualities. The second verb has the same minuita sequence as the first, not OCR miniuita. The Portuguese context expects Eu sei, “I know,” but the enlarged initial is F-shaped with no secure lower E arm: retain the source-facing Fu ſei and flag the anomaly rather than silently repairing it.

runs.text: todo o interior, & quanto ha na quelle homem.

lines.note: The translation continues “all the interior, and all that is in that man,” confirming the sense of penetrating insight. The printed separation na quelle and unaccented ha are retained.
Minzocu is the common people, further specified as farmers. The separate Minzu. below this last body row is a catchword, not an additional definition or continuation.
